title: Grove's Coltrane comparison and recognition with Elvin
summary: Early Trane contains Prez, Ammons and Dexter; he was noticed as a soloist with Elvin more than in Buddy's big band.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Nice. Well I’ll read what they said. They should have called you. In regards to your style, “His style is derived principally from that of John Coltrane to which he adds his own rhythmic looseness and lyricism.

Yeah I mean you listen to early Trane and it’s Prez and it’s Gene Ammons and it’s Dexter you know. I mean they’re all in there. I mean everybody’s kind of mixed up in there. But I mean the time that I was probably being more recognized for my soloing would have been with Elvin Jones. With Buddy of course I was known as a soloist but with a big band you’re only going to get a small chunk of space to solo. Right? Maybe one big feature that you get that you know — the suite was something that I kind of inherited from Don Menza. And so with Elvin’s band, when they heard me play, and those articles were probably written back then, I was heavily into those by Trane. It’s pretty hard not to go down that road when you’re playing with Elvin, and then especially when you’re playing with Elvin and McCoy and Reggie Workman. All of the sudden there’s that trio behind you and, you know, I’m going to come out and play like Zoot Sims it just didn’t fit the flow of where I felt the time was. And I wanted to study and I learned that music. I used to go see Coltrane all the time when I was in Rochester or going to Berklee. That was one of the things you did. When he came to town you went down to see him.
